05-00-00-910-802Airworthiness Limitation PrecautionsPDF p. 65
1. Airworthiness Limitation Precautions
A. General
(1) Critical Design Configuration Control Limitations (CDCCLs)
(a) All occurrences of CDCCLs found in this chapter of the AMM are identified by this note
after each applicable CDCCL design feature:
1) NOTE: CDCCL - Refer to the task: Airworthiness Limitation Precautions,
TASK 05-00-00-910-802, for important information on Critical Design Configuration
Control Limitations (CDCCLs).
(b) Design features that are CDCCLs are defined and controlled by Special Federal Aviation
Regulation (SFAR) 88, and can be found in Section 9 of the Maintenance Planning Data
(MPD) document. CDCCLs are a means of identifying certain design configuration
features intended to preclude a fuel tank ignition source for the operational life of the
airplane. CDCCLs are mandatory and cannot be changed or deleted without the approval
of the FAA Oversight Office that is responsible for the airplane model Type Certificate. A
critical fuel tank ignition source prevention feature may exist in the fuel system and its
related installation or in systems that, if a failure condition were to develop, could interact
with the fuel system in such a way that an unsafe condition would develop without this
limitation. Strict adherence to configuration, methods, techniques, and practices as
prescribed is required to ensure the CDCCL is complied with. Any use of parts, methods,
techniques or practices not contained in the applicable CDCCL must be approved by the
FAA Oversight Office that is responsible for the airplane model Type Certificate.
(2) Airworthiness Limitation Instructions (ALIs)
(a) All occurrences of fuel tank system ALIs found in this chapter of the AMM are identified
by this note after each applicable ALI inspection feature:
1) NOTE ALI - Refer to the task: Airworthiness Limitation Precautions,
TASK 05-00-00-910-802, for important information on airworthiness limitation
instructions (ALIs).
(b) Inspection features that are ALIs are defined and controlled by Special Federal Aviation
Regulation (SFAR) 88, and can be found in Section 9 of the Maintenance Planning Data
(MPD) document. These ALIs identify inspection features related to fuel tank ignition
source prevention which must be done to maintain the design level of safety for the
operational life of the airplane. These inspection features are mandatory and cannot be
changed or deleted without the approval of the FAA Oversight Office that is responsible
for the airplane model Type Certificate. Strict adherence to methods, techniques and
practices as prescribed is required to ensure the ALI is complied with. Any use of
methods, techniques or practices not contained in these ALIs must be approved by the
FAA Oversight Office that is responsible for the airplane model Type Certificate.
B. Location Zones
Zone Area
100 Lower Half of Fuselage
200 Upper Half of Fuselage
500 Left Wing
600 Right Wing
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL

05-00-00-910-804Enhanced Zonal Inspection Program (EZAP) PrecautionsPDF p. 66
2. Enhanced Zonal Inspection Program (EZAP) Precautions
A. General
(1) Enhanced Zonal Analysis Procedure (EZAP) and associated Electrical Wiring Interconnection
System (EWIS)
(a) Enhanced Zonal Analysis Procedure (EZAP) is an analytical procedure required by Part
25, Appendix H, Section H25.5(a)(1) that identifies the physical and environmental
conditions contained in each zone of an airplane, analyzes the effects of these conditions
on electrical wiring and components, and assesses the possibilities for smoke and fire.
The end result of the analysis are inspection and restoration tasks in the form of EWIS
ICA.
(b) Electrical Wiring Interconnection System (EWIS): means any wire, power feeder, wiring
device, or combination of these, including termination devices, installed in any area of the
airplane for the purpose of transmitting electrical energy, including data and signals,
between two or more intended termination points. EWIS is defined in full by 14 CFR
section 25.1701.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(c) The Zonal Inspection Program includes a general visual and, if required, physical check
of the general condition and security of attachment of the accessible systems and
structures items contained in defined zones. This includes checks for degradation such
as chafing of tubing, loose duct supports, damage to wiring and connected EWIS, cable
and pulley wear, fluid leaks, electrical bonding, general condition of fasteners, inadequate
drainage, etc., and general corrosion, not covered in the MSG-3 analysis. The zonal
inspection is not intended as a quality assurance after maintenance check for
determining proper reassembly of systems, components, structures, or powerplants. The
zonal program packages a number of General Visual (GV) Inspections into one or more
zonal inspections. The program includes any GV inspection tasks required to assure
security of attachment and general condition of any system or structural items within the
zone.
(2) Equivalent Tools, Fixtures, Test Equipment, and Consumable Materials
(a) When the procedures in this manual identify tools, equipment, and consumable materials,
you can use equivalent alternatives. If you use alternative tools, equipment, or
consumable materials, make sure that they give the same results and are as safe to the
parts and personnel as the tools, equipment, or consumable materials specified in the
procedure.
B. References
Reference Title
20-60-07-913-801 Protection of the EWIS During Maintenance (P/B 201)
C. Protection of EWIS During Maintenance, Repair and Alterations
SUBTASK 05-00-00-910-006
WARNING
OBEY THE MANUFACTURER'S PROCEDURES WHEN YOU DO EZAP
MAINTENANCE, OR MAINTENANCE THAT HAS AN EFFECT ON EWIS. IF
YOU DO NOT OBEY THE PROCEDURES, IT CAN INCREASE THE RISK OF
AN IGNITION SOURCE FOR FIRES. INJURIES TO PERSONS, AND DAMAGE
TO EQUIPMENT CAN OCCUR.
(1) Make sure you follow the procedures for items identified as EZAP.
(2) Refer to Protection of the EWIS During Maintenance, TASK 20-60-07-913-801.

SUBTASK 05-41-01-211-002
(1) Perform a detailed inspection of the Center Wing Rear Spar Vapor Web for cracking in the

(2) Open these access panels:
Number Name/Location

834AZ Aft Entry Door - Torque Tube Access
834BZ Aft Entry Door - Handle Box and Cam for Handle Box Access
834CZ Aft Entry Door - Handle Box Access

 ALL
(a) Remove a pressure fay surface seal that was previously applied between the mating
surfaces of the cover plate and the inner skin (SOPM 20-50-19).
(b) Remove a parting agent that was previously applied on the mating surfaces of the cover
plate (SOPM 20-50-19).

Number Name/Location

834GZ AFT Entry Door - Torque Tube Access
(a) Apply a parting agent to the mating surfaces of the cover plate (SOPM 20-50-19).
(b) Apply a pressure fay surface seal with sealant, A00247, between the mating surfaces of
the cover plate and the inner skin (SOPM 20-50-19).
(c) Install the cover plate onto the door structure with the bolts and the washers.
1) If a new bolt is to be used, make sure that the grip length is the same as the original
bolt.
NOTE: Grip length is important.

(a) Apply a parting agent to the mating surfaces of the cover plate (SOPM 20-50-19).

the cover plate and the inner skin (SOPM 20-50-19).

bolt.

C. Nose Landing Gear and Forward Fuselage Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-040
(1) Perform the Nose Landing Gear (NLG) and forward fuselage inspection procedure as stated in
PAGEBLOCK 05-51-37/201, if it was a “Hard Nose Gear Landing”, or a “High Drag or High
Side Load Condition”.
D. Main Landing Gear Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-041
(1) Examine the Main Landing Gear (MLG) areas as follows (Figure 203, Figure 204):
(a) The tires for damage (TASK 32-45-00-700-803).
(b) The wheels for damage; cracks, missing tie-bolts, heat shield (TASK 32-45-00-700-801).
(c) The shock struts at the top and bottom end for signs of fluid leakage.
NOTE: A small quantity of hydraulic fluid on the inner cylinder is satisfactory.
(d) The top end of the shock strut for cracks and bolt distortion.
(e) The outer door and linkage.
(f) The center door and linkage.
(g) The inner door and linkage.
(h) The trunnions and shock strut top end, including bushing edges/flanges and visible pin's
external surface plating.
(i) The side strut and trunnion attach fittings of the main landing gear.
(j) The landing gear walking beam to wing structure attachment fittings.
(k) The landing gear trunnion to landing gear walking beam attachment and landing gear
trunnion to wing structure.
(l) The landing gear beam.
(m) The main landing beam outboard support fitting.
(n) The forward trunnion support fitting.
(o) The main landing gear beam inboard support (hanger link fitting).
(p) If the airplane departs the prepared surface, do the inspections outlined in Phase IB.
E. Fuselage, Wing, Empennage and Engine Strut/Nacelle Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-042
(1) Examine the fuselage areas that follow:
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(a) Examine the upper and lower fuselage skin panels forward and aft of the wing.
NOTE: Permanent wrinkles frequently occur on the lower side of the fuselage skins aft of
STA 727.
(b) If you found wrinkles on the skin panels and you did not know they were there before,
make an internal inspection.
NOTE: If the wrinkles were there before, make a careful inspection of the wrinkles for
cracks.
(c) Examine the keel beam chords, stiffeners, webs and splices at station 663 thru 727A.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-056
(2) Perform a general visual examination of the areas around the probes and static ports.
(a) If obvious visual damage is found, do an RVSM check: SRM 51-10-03.
(3) Examine the wing lower surface leading edge, inspar, and trailing edge for signs of damage.
F. Cabin Inspections
NOTE: If inspections of the forward cabin were already performed during Phase I Inspection,
TASK 05-51-37-200-806, then they do not need to be repeated.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-043
(1) Do the following cabin inspections that follow to find possible damage:
(a) Do a visual inspection of all ceiling panels (and video monitors, if applicable) for
dislodging and evidence due to impact damage.
(b) Do a visual inspection of all overhead bins for evidence of looseness and impact
damage.
(2) If any cabin damage was found in the Phase IA Cabin Inspections including the ceiling panels,
overhead bins, or the video monitors then continue the Cabin Inspection in Phase IB and
Phase II. If no damage was found, no further cabin inspections are required, and it is not
necessary to continue the cabin inspections in Phase IB and Phase II.
05-51-01-210-805Phase IB InspectionPDF p. 839

E. Main Landing Gear Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-044
(1) Examine the main landing gear areas as follows:
(a) Examine the tires for damage (Tires - Inspection, TASK 32-45-00-700-803)
(b) Examine the wheels for damage; cracks, missing tie-bolts, heat shield (Wheels Fast
Check (Wheel Installed on the Airplane), TASK 32-45-00-700-801)
(c) Examine the brake assemblies for damage (Main Landing Gear Brake Fast Check
(Wheel Installed on the Airplane), TASK 32-41-41-700-802)
(d) The shock strut of the main gear for fluid leakage (top & bottom)
(e) The doors and linkages of the main gear strut
(f) The landing gear beam and attachment fittings
(g) Remove the forward trunnion fuse pin [5] and perform a detailed visual inspection if any
of the following events occurred such that a significant drag loading on the main gear is
expected:
1) The main landing gear hit an obstacle of large mass, or
2) The aircraft landed short of the prepared surface, or
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
3) The airplane ran off the prepared surface which produced a peak deceleration that
was more severe than maximum effort braking.
NOTE: Inspection of the forward trunnion fuse pins may be deferred for
non-revenue ferry flights only.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-074
(2) If the airplane departs off the prepared surface, do the following:
(a) Examine the tires for damage (Tires - Inspection, TASK 32-45-00-700-803)
(b) Examine the wheels for damage; cracks, missing tiebolts, heat shield (Wheels Fast
Check (Wheel Installed on the Airplane), TASK 32-45-00-700-801)
1) After the examination, if the tires and wheels have not been damaged, do these
steps:
a) Do the recovery and/or movement of the airplane to the prepared surface.
2) If the wheel heat shield(s) is/are bent and prevents the free rotation of the wheel
and the tire assembly that contacts the brake:
a) Bend the heat shield(s) to allow free rotation of the wheel and tire assembly.
NOTE: The airplane can be towed to a location where further inspections and
examinations will be performed.
3) After the examination, if the tires and wheels are determined to be damaged and
prevents the recovery and/or movement of the airplane to the prepared surface, do
these steps:
a) Replace the wheel and tire assemblies to allow recovery and movement of the
airplane (MAIN LANDING GEAR WHEEL AND TIRE ASSEMBLY -
REMOVAL/INSTALLATION, PAGEBLOCK 32-45-11/401).
4) Examine the brake assemblies for damage (Main Landing Gear Brake Fast Check
(Wheel Installed on the Airplane), TASK 32-41-41-700-802)
a) If a brake assembly is damaged and does not allow the rotation of the wheel
and tire assembly, do these steps:
NOTE: If the wheel and tire assembly cannot rotate because the brake
assembly is damaged, the brake assembly must be removed. After the
brake assembly is removed and the wheel and tire assembly is
installed, then the airplane can be towed safely.
<1> Remove the Wheel and Tire assembly (Main Landing Gear Wheel and
Tire Assembly Removal, TASK 32-45-11-000-801).
<2> Remove the brake assembly (Main Landing Gear Brake Removal,
TASK 32-41-41-000-801).
<3> Install the Wheel and Tire assembly (Main Landing Gear Wheel and
Tire Assembly Installation, TASK 32-45-11-400-801).
NOTE: The wheel and tire assembly is installed to allow the airplane to
be recovered.
5) After the airplane has been moved to a location for further examination, and before
next flight, do these steps:
a) Replace the damaged wheel and tire assemblies (MAIN LANDING GEAR
WHEEL AND TIRE ASSEMBLY - REMOVAL/INSTALLATION,
PAGEBLOCK 32-45-11/401)
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
<1> If the wheel and tire assemblies were replaced before the airplane
recovery. Clean the wheel and tire assemblies of unwanted material.
<2> After the wheel and tire assemblies have been cleaned, examine the
wheels and tires for damage (Tires - Inspection,
TASK 32-45-00-700-803, Wheels Fast Check (Wheel Installed on the
Airplane), TASK 32-45-00-700-801).
<3> If no damage is found, the wheels and tires are serviceable.
b) Prior to flight, replace the brake assemblies (MAIN LANDING GEAR BRAKE -
REMOVAL/INSTALLATION, PAGEBLOCK 32-41-41/401).
c) Remove the brake sleeves and examine the axles.
NOTE: There are occasions where the airplane lands and one Main Landing
Gear (MLG) departs the prepared surface but then returns to the
prepared surface and taxis to the gate. In this case, the wheel/tire￾and brake-assemblies need to be cleaned of any debris and
examined.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-075
(3) During a landing, if one main landing gear departs from the prepared surface and returns to
the prepared surface and taxis to the gate, do these steps:
(a) Examine the tires for damage (Tires - Inspection, TASK 32-45-00-700-803)
(b) Examine the wheels for damage; cracks, missing tiebolts, heat shield (Wheels Fast
Check (Wheel Installed on the Airplane), TASK 32-45-00-700-801)
(c) Examine the brake assemblies for damage (Main Landing Gear Brake Fast Check
(Wheel Installed on the Airplane), TASK 32-41-41-700-802)
F. Nose Landing Gear Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-045
(1) Perform the NOSE LANDING GEAR AND FORWARD FUSELAGE - MAINTENANCE
PRACTICES (CONDITIONAL INSPECTION), PAGEBLOCK 05-51-37/201, if it was a "Hard
Nose Gear Landing", or a "High Drag or High Side Load Condition".
G. Fuselage Inspection
NOTE: If inspections of the forward fuselage were already performed during Nose Gear and
Forward Fuselage NOSE LANDING GEAR AND FORWARD FUSELAGE - MAINTENANCE
PRACTICES (CONDITIONAL INSPECTION), PAGEBLOCK 05-51-37/201, then they do not
need to be repeated.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-200-003
(1) Examine the aft side of the pressure bulkhead for signs of buckling, deformation or damage.
(a) Do a detailed visual inspection of the entire aft side of the BS 1016 aft pressure
bulkhead. Give particular attention to the upper bulkhead structure between skin stringers
S-10L and S-10R.
NOTE: Access to the interior unpressurized aft pressure bulkhead area is through the aft
access hatch, 311BL.
H. Wing Area Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-860-001
(1) Extend the Trailing Edge (TE) flaps, do this task: Extend the Trailing Edge Flaps,
TASK 27-51-00-860-803.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
SUBTASK 05-51-01-860-002
(2) Extend the Leading Edge (LE) flaps and slats, do this task: Leading Edge Flaps and Slats
Extension, TASK 27-81-00-860-803.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-040-007
WARNING
DO THE DEACTIVATION PROCEDURE FOR THE TRAILING EDGE FLAP
BEFORE YOU DO WORK ON THE FLAP SYSTEM. THE FLAPS MOVE
QUICKLY. THEY CAN CAUSE INJURIES TO PERSONNEL, AND DAMAGE TO
EQUIPMENT.
(3) Do this task: Trailing Edge Flap System Deactivation, TASK 27-51-00-040-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-040-012
WARNING
DO THE DEACTIVATION PROCEDURE FOR THE LEADING EDGE FLAPS
AND SLATS. THE FLAPS AND SLATS MOVE QUICKLY. INJURIES TO
PERSONNEL, AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT CAN OCCUR.
(4) (Preferred Configuration) If the LE flaps and slat locks are available, do these steps to secure
the area under the wing for inspection:
(a) Do this task: Leading Edge Flaps and Slats Deactivation, TASK 27-81-00-040-801.
(b) Do this task: Leading Edge Flap and Slat Locks Installation, TASK 27-81-00-480-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-01-040-013
WARNING
DO THE ALTERNATIVE DEACTIVATION PROCEDURE FOR THE LEADING
EDGE FLAPS AND SLATS. THE FLAPS AND SLATS MOVE QUICKLY. IF YOU
DO NOT OBEY, INJURIES TO PERSONNEL, AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT
CAN OCCUR.
(5) (Alternate Configuration) If the LE flaps and slat locks are not available, do these steps to
secure the area under the wing for inspection:
NOTE: This alternate method is used to secure the areas under the wing leading edge and
trailing edge when no other maintenance action or structural inspection is required,
scheduled or unscheduled.
(a) Do these steps to secure the hydraulic system:
1) Make sure that the hydraulic power is removed (TASK 29-11-00-860-805).
2) Make sure that the HYD PUMPS A ELEC 2 and the HYD PUMPS B ELEC 1
switches are in the OFF position.
3) Make sure that the HYD PUMPS ENG switch is in the ON position.
NOTE: The HYD PUMPS ENG switch should be left in the ON position. This will
increase the life of the depressurization solenoid which becomes energized
when the HYD PUMPS ENG switch is put in the OFF position.
4) Attach a DO NOT OPERATE tag, STD-858, on the HYD PUMPS switches.
(b) Make sure that the Proximity Sensor Electronics Unit (PSEU) is in GROUND MODE
(TASK 32-09-00-860-802).
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(c) Open this circuit breaker and install safety tag:
F/O Electrical System Panel, P6-2
Row Col Number Name
A 7 C00210 FLIGHT CONTROL FLAP SHUTOFF VALVES
(d) Make sure that the ALTERNATE FLAP ARM switch is in the OFF position.
(e) Attach a DO NOT OPERATE tag, STD-858, on the flap control lever and the ALTERNATE
FLAPS ARM switch.
(f) Do these steps to secure the LE Uncommanded Motion (UCM) shutoff valve:
1) Open this access panel:
Number Name/Location
192BR ECS Ram Air Inlet Mixing Duct Panel - Forward
2) Remove the lockwire from the manual override lever (handle).
3) Move the manual override lever on the LE UCM shutoff valve to the OFF position.
NOTE: The lever should move with very little force. If the lever is tight, you may
need hydraulic pressure and the Flap/Slat Electronics Unit (FSEU) to
release the pressure on the LE UCM shutoff valve.
4) Install the lockout pin, SPL-1746, in the manual override lever to keep the lever in
the OFF position.
a) If the tool cannot be easily installed then it is necessary to supply system B
hydraulic power and then use the FSEU to relieve the pressure on the LE
UCM shutoff valve.
<1> Use the FSEU procedure below but replace the selection of the LE
DEPR valve for the LE UCM shutoff valve.
NOTE: Two persons will be necessary when the FSEU is used to
operate the LE UCM shutoff valve.
5) Attach a DO-NOT-REMOVE tag on the rig pin or lockout pin, SPL-1746.
(g) Do these steps to secure the LE cruise depressurization valve (located in the main
landing gear wheel well):
1) If the valve has a tab, cut the tab from the valve (SB 27-1242).
2) Remove the lockwire from the manual override lever (handle).
3) Move the manual override lever up to the OFF position.
NOTE: Do not force movement of the lever with tools. The lever should move with
very little force. If the lever is tight, you may need hydraulic pressure and
the FSEU to relieve the pressure on the LE cruise depressurization valve.
a) If you cannot move the manual override lever, use the FSEU and hydraulic
pressure to operate the LE cruise depressurization valve.
NOTE: Two persons will be necessary when the FSEU is used to operate the
LE cruise depressurization valve.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
WARNING
KEEP PERSONS AND EQUIPMENT CLEAR OF THE
FLIGHT CONTROL SURFACES, THE THRUST
REVERSERS, AND THE LANDING GEAR. THESE
COMPONENTS CAN MOVE SUDDENLY WHEN YOU
SUPPLY HYDRAULIC POWER. THIS CAN CAUSE
INJURIES TO PERSONS AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT.
<1> Supply system B hydraulic power (TASK 29-11-00-860-801).
<2> Use the FSEU to release the pressure on the LE cruise
depressurization valve, as follows:
<a> Get access to the main equipment center, open this access
panel:

117A Electronic Equipment Access Door
<b> Remove the safety tag and close this circuit breaker:

A 7 C00210 FLIGHT CONTROL FLAP
SHUTOFF VALVES

<j> SET ON..... press YES.
<3> Move the manual override lever up to the OFF position.
4) Install the lockout pin, SPL-1746, in the manual override lever to keep the lever in

NOTE: If the newer -1003 cruise depressurization valve is installed on the airplane
then the lockout pin, SPL-1746, will stop the movement of the leading edge

EFFECTIVITY

WARNING
IF A -1001 CRUISE DEPRESSURIZATION VALVE IS INSTALLED,
DO NOT APPLY HYDRAULIC POWER TO EXTEND OR
RETRACT THE TRAILING EDGE WHEN THE LEADING EDGE
FLAPS ARE DEACTIVATED. A -1001 VALVE CAN HAVE
HYDRAULIC PRESSURE LEAKAGE AND WILL NOT STOP THE
MOVEMENT OF THE LEADING EDGE FLAPS AND SLATS.
MOVEMENT OF THE LEADING EDGE FLAPS AND SLATS CAN
CAUSE DAMAGE TO AN OPEN THRUST REVERSER AND
INJURY TO PERSONNEL.
a) If the older -1001 cruise depressurization valve is installed on the airplane, do
these steps:
NOTE: A leading edge device creep condition has been associated with a “lap
assembly” tolerances or a combination of “lap assembly” tolerances
and the use of the smaller 0.3125 in. (7.9375 mm) diameter lockout
pin, SPL-1746, that could be the cause of hydraulic pressure leakage
through the older -1001 valve.
<1> Make sure that the hydraulic power is turned OFF after the leading
edge devices have been moved to their desired position.
<2> Make sure to attach the DO NOT OPERATE tag, STD-858, to both
ELEC 1 and the ELEC 2 HYD PUMP switches on the P5 panel.
NOTE: Due to -1001 cruise depressurization valve installed, hydraulics
cannot be operated until LE flaps and slats are re-activated.
5) Attach a DO-NOT-REMOVE tag on the rig pin or lockout pin, SPL-1746.
6) If the FSEU was used, then do the following:
a) Remove system B hydraulic power (TASK 29-11-00-860-805).
b) Open this circuit breaker and install safety tag:
F/O Electrical System Panel, P6-2
Row Col Number Name
A 7 C00210 FLIGHT CONTROL FLAP SHUTOFF VALVES
(h) Do these steps to prevent leading edge devices extension or retraction by the standby
hydraulic system:
1) Disconnect the electrical connector from the LE standby drive shutoff valve.
a) After you disconnect the electrical connector, examine the connector for
corrosion.
NOTE: The inspection of the electrical connector(s) can be done after the
removal step or before the installation step of the electrical connector.
This is an operator option.
b) If there was corrosion, correct the problem (SWPM 20-60-03).
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
WARNING
MAKE SURE THAT THE MANUAL OVERRIDE LEVER IS IN

EDGE SLATS. IF THE LEADING EDGE SLATS MOVE, DAMAGE TO
AN OPEN THRUST REVERSER AND INJURIES TO PERSONNEL
CAN OCCUR.
2) Make sure that the override lever is in the Position 1 (standby hydraulic power
OFF).
NOTE: If the manual override lever at the LE standby drive shutoff valve is in
Position 2 and the standby hydraulic system is then pressurized, the
leading edge slats will move to the full extend position.
3) Install the lockout pin, SPL-1746.
NOTE: The lock, SPL-1675, can be used on the standby hydraulic system for the

4) Attach a DO NOT OPERATE tag, STD-858, on the LE standby drive shutoff valve.
(i) Do the LE flaps and slats tryout (TASK 27-81-00-040-801).

D. Main Landing Gear Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-01-210-005
(1) Examine the Main Landing Gear (MLG) areas as follows (Figure 203, Figure 204).
(a) Examine the outer and inner cylinder lugs.
(b) Examine the trunnion fitting area of the outer cylinder including the bushing
edges/flanges.
(c) Examine the torsion links.
(d) Examine the actuator walking beam and linkage fittings.
(e) Examine the MLG beam fitting and AFT trunnion support fitting on the shock strut for
cracks.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(f) Examine these MLG pins and fuse pins: side strut hanger link assembly pin [1], side strut
hanger link pin [2], side strut pin [3], fuse pin [4], fuse pin [5], upper hanger link pin [6],
pin [7], lower hanger link pin [8], aft trunnion pin [9], and fwd trunnion pin [10].
1) For vertical overload remove the MLG Beam outboard attachment fuse pin [4] and
perform a detailed visual inspection.
a) Remove the MLG (TASK 32-11-00-000-801).
b) Remove the MLG support beam as required (TASK 57-15-00-000-801).
c) If damage is found remove the forward trunnion fuse pins and perform a
detailed visual inspection.
2) For a high drag or high side load overload, remove the forward trunnion fuse pins
and perform a detailed visual inspection.
a) Remove the MLG (TASK 32-11-00-000-801).
b) Remove the MLG support beam as required (TASK 57-15-00-000-801).
c) If damage is found remove MLG Beam outboard attachment fuse pin and
perform a detailed visual inspection.
(g) Make sure that the pressure and hydraulic fluid levels in the main landing gear shock
struts are correct, do this task: Main Landing Gear Shock Strut Fluid Check,
TASK 12-15-31-610-801.
1) If the fluid level is low; do these steps:
a) Do this task: Replace the Active Seals with the Spare Seals,
TASK 32-11-21-960-801.
b) Remove the inner cylinder and examine it for distortions or cracks, do this
task: Landing Gear Inner Cylinder Chrome Inspection,
TASK 32-00-10-211-801.
c) Examine the orifice support tube, while it is on the airplane, for cracks.
(h) Examine the wheel well of the main landing gear for fuel or other fluid leaks.
(i) If a high drag or side load condition, and a hard landing occur at the same time, remove
the main gear inner cylinders, do this task: Landing Gear Inner Cylinder Chrome
Inspection, TASK 32-00-10-211-801.
1) Look for distortions or cracks in the inner cylinder.
(j) Examine the side strut and side strut attachments.
(k) If any main landing gear wheels are removed because of a blown tire, do the steps that
follow:
1) Examine the wheel structure for damage.
2) Examine the brake assembly for damage (TASK 32-41-41-700-803).

 ALL

(c) Do this task: Nose Landing Gear Torsional Freeplay Inspection, TASK 32-21-00-700-801.
(d) Examine the nose landing gear wheel well.
(e) Examine the drag strut support fittings.
(f) Examine the outer-cylinder-trunnion-fitting area and the drag brace linkage.

D. Severe or Unusual Turbulence Condition
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-016
(1) Severe turbulence is identified as turbulence which causes large, abrupt changes in the
altitude and/or attitude. The airplane could be out of control for short periods. It usually causes
large variations in airspeed. Passengers and crew are moved violently against their seat belts
and loose objects are moved around the airplane.
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-024
(2) An inspection is required when the aircraft has encountered severe turbulence. The pilot must
report the suspected encounter of this event. If the pilot reports that the aircraft has
encountered severe turbulence, refer to “Examine Airplane Structure and Wing Areas” and
“Cabin Inspections” in this section.
E. Excessive Maneuver Condition
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-018
(1) Excessive maneuvers are maneuvers that result in severe and abnormal aircraft response
and/or attitude, and/or exceeding of the flight maneuvering vertical load factors, specified
below. Excessive maneuvers could be due to rapid or large alternating control inputs i.e.,
control column, rudder pedals, and control wheel.
(a) The vertical acceleration load limits shown below are directly applicable to excessive
maneuvers.
1) Flaps up . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 2.5g to -1.0g
2) Flaps down . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 2.0g to 0.0g
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-025
(2) An inspection is required when the aircraft has been involved in an excessive maneuver. The
pilot must report the suspected encounter of this event. If the pilot reports that the airplane has
been involved in an excessive maneuver, refer to "Examine Airplane Structure and Wing
Areas" and "Cabin Inspections" in this section.
F. Severe or Unusual Buffet Condition
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-002
(1) If an unusual vibration, an unusual maneuver or a severe or unusual buffet condition occurs
in-flight, do the "Examine the Airplane Structure and Wing Areas" steps in the following task:
Severe or Unusual Turbulence, Excessive Maneuver, Buffet, or Speeds More than the Design
Limits Conditional Inspection, TASK 05-51-04-210-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-003
(2) If a stall occurs after the initial buffet or stick shaker condition, an inspection is necessary.
(a) Do the Stall (After Initial Buffet or Stick Shaker) Structural Inspection Procedure.
G. Airplane Speeds More than the Design Limits
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-004
(1) The maximum design speed of the airplane for flight operations are as follows:
NOTE: The Maximum Operating Limit Speed is in Section 1, LIMITATIONS of the Airplane
Flight Manual (AFM).
(a) The airplane Maximum Operating Speed (VMO) is 340 knots (630 km/h) when the
airplane is at or below 25,968 ft (7915 m).
(b) Above 25,968 ft (7915 m), the airplane is limited to a Maximum Operating Mach (MMO)
of 0.82.
(c) The overspeed clacker will activate when the airplane exceeds the VMO or MMO.
SUBTASK 05-51-04-210-005
(2) Do the “Examine the Airplane Structure and Wing Areas” procedure in the task if one or both
conditions that follow occurs:
NOTE: When the overspeed event occurs at 25,968 ft (7915 m) or below, it should be viewed
in knots. Overspeed events above 25,968 ft (7915 m) should be viewed in mach.
(a) The airplane speed exceeds the VMO by 20 knots (37 km/h) or more.
(b) The airplane speed exceeds the MMO by 0.02 Mach or more.

05-51-07-210-801High Energy StopPDF p. 867
2. High Energy Stop
A. General
(1) The level of the inspection depends on the level of absorbed kinetic energy.
(2) High energy stop is an event where the brake energy falls within the "Caution" or "Fuse Plug
Melt" zones.
(3) The heat absorbed by the airplane brake is slowly, but not fully transmitted to the wheel, tire,
axle, and in-axle components.
(4) The wheels have fuse plugs which are designed to melt and release the tire pressure.
NOTE: The fuse plugs melt at a specific design temperature.
(a) This is to stop ruptures of the tires and wheels when the wheel temperature gets too high.
(5) If brake fire occurs, do the steps in the "High Energy Stop Condition Inspection - IN FUSE
PLUG MELT range or Brake Fire" section.
(6) The brake cooling time starts once the airplane is stationary and no further brake applications
are performed.
(7) Use the brake energy chart to approximate energy absorbed by a brake unit (Figure 202 or
Figure 203).
(a) This chart will give only the approximate energy absorbed during the stop.
1) The factors that follow will also affect the energy absorbed:
a) The residual energy from the previous stop
b) The runway slope
c) The wind conditions
d) The thrust reverser use.
(b) Listed below are example values to show you how to use the Brake Energy Chart to
obtain result values (Figure 201):
NOTE: The brake temperature monitoring system (BTMS) indications are also shown in
the bottom of the figure. If brake cooling is determined from the BTMS, use the
hottest brake indication 10 to 15 minutes after the airplane has come to a
complete stop, or in-flight with gear retracted to determine recommended cooling
schedule.
NOTE: The data values given below are for example only and must not be used to
determine a specific airplane absorbed energy by a brake unit. The airplane
operators must use actual values generated by the specific airplane high energy
stop/heat event.
1) Example input values:
a) Gross Weight - 135,000 lb (61,235 kg)
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
b) Brakes on Speed - 120 knots (222 km/h) (no wind)
c) Pressure Altitude - 5000 ft (2 km)
d) Outside Air Temperature - 80°F (27°C)
e) Landing stop using maximum manual braking
f) No Thrust Reversers.
2) Example result values:
a) Resultant Brake Energy - 26,000,000 ft-lb (35,251,268 N·m)
b) Resultant is in the COOLING RECOMMENDED range.
(8) A high energy condition can be a refused takeoff.
(a) It can also be any stop or sequence of stops that collect energy in the CAUTION or FUSE
PLUG MELT range (Figure 202 or Figure 203).
(9) An indication that a high energy stop, or equivalent, has occurred is the release of a wheel
fuse plug.
NOTE: If fuse plug releases do occur, the condition is a high energy stop within the fuse plug
melt range.
(a) Energy levels are different between brakes after stops in the COOLING
RECOMMENDED range.
(b) One or more brakes could have absorbed energy in the CAUTION range, and one or
more wheel fuse plugs released.
(10) For main landing gear tires that have been subjected to unusual service events, such as high
energy rejected takeoffs, high energy stops, or high energy overspeed landings where thermal
fuse plugs have melted, these tires should be removed and discarded. If the main landing gear
tires on the airplane remain inflated, remove the wheel-tire assembly and send the hardware to
your local wheel shop for the inspection.
(a) Make sure to identify all tires of the unusual service event when returning the tires to the
supplier.
(11) If the nose and main landing gear tires exceed their respective tire speed rating during the
overspeed landing, remove the wheel-tire assembly and send the hardware to your local wheel
shop for inspection.
(a) Make sure to identify all tires of the unusual service event when returning the tires to the
supplier.

1) If a fuse plug has melted, do the FUSE PLUG MELT Range inspection.

05-51-07-280-801Heat Damage Inspection (Ammonium Persulfate Solution)PDF p. 878
3. Heat Damage Inspection (Ammonium Persulfate Solution)
A. General
(1) This inspection is used to find if the high strength steel that showed visible signs of heat
damage, had changed.
(a) It will look for a change in the temper or heat treat properties.
NOTE: Refer to product Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) and local requirements for
proper handling procedures.
(2) This inspection will usually occur on the components of the landing gear axles.
(a) The signs of discolored or blistered paint or plating shows that a general intense heat has
changed the temper of the axle.
1) When this happens, the ammonium persulfate procedure should be applied to the
damaged part of the axle.

SUBTASK 05-51-07-120-001
(1) Do the steps that follow to apply the solution, ammonium persulfate compound, G02412.
NOTE: 100 grams of ammonium persulfate per 0.27 gal (1.02 l) of tap water will make the

 ALL
WARNING

GET IT IN YOUR EYES, ON YOUR SKIN, OR ON YOUR CLOTHES.
INJURY TO PERSONS CAN OCCUR.
(a) Remove the paint from the heat damage areas.
(b) Strip the cadmium surface with sandpaper, abrasive cloth, B00102 applied by hand.
1) Strip a minimum area of 0.5 in. (12.7 mm) larger than the area that is to be tested.

SOLUTIONS. DO NOT GET THEM IN YOUR EYES, ON YOUR SKIN OR

CADMIUM PLATED SURFACES. POISONOUS FUMES CAN OCCUR. IT

SUBTASK 05-51-07-210-003
(1) Do the steps that follow to examine the etched areas:
(a) Examine the parts with a bright light and without magnification.
1) Look for signs of heat damage.
(b) If all of the etched area is the same shade of gray, there was no change to the temper of
the steel.
(c) If the area has been too hot it will be a lighter or darker color than the normal color.
NOTE: Darker color shows over-tempered martensite.
NOTE: Darker color in a lighter circle shows untempered martensite surrounded by
overtempered material.
(d) If the etched area is mottled (has spots or streaks of a different color), the condition of the
heat treat will be unknown.
NOTE: If this condition occurs, replace the axle.

 ALL

2. Phase I Inspection
A. Airplane Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-09-212-003
(1) Do the inspection of the main and nose landing gear.
(a) Examine all tires and wheels.
(b) Examine the support structure.
(c) Look for signs of fluid leakage at the top and bottom of the outer cylinder of the shock
strut.
NOTE: A small quantity of hydraulic fluid on the surface of the inner cylinder of the shock
strut is satisfactory.
SUBTASK 05-51-09-212-004
(2) Do the inspection of the landing gear, fuselage, and wing.
(a) Look for fuel leaks, and other fluid leaks, in the areas that follow:
1) All wheel well areas of the body, wing, and nose landing gear.
2) The lower external surface of the fuselage in the area of the wing-to-body fairing.
3) The wing.

(b) Examine carefully these components (Body Stations 540 through 727A):

2) Stiffeners

were not there before the landing. Examine the wrinkles carefully for cracks.

05-51-12-110-801Toilet Over-Servicing Condition - CleaningPDF p. 911
2. Toilet Over-Servicing Condition - Cleaning
A. General
(1) If blue water contamination is found in the airplane, after an over-servicing event has occurred,
an immediate cleanup action is necessary to prevent possible contamination of electrical or
electronic components.
(2) It is possible for blue water contamination to occur in a single isolated area or more than one
area, dependent upon the amount of liquid spilled. All contaminated areas are to be completely
cleaned.
(3) It is most important that all moisture is removed from the contaminated area. Clean cloths and
dry air are to be used.
(4) In all areas where blue water contamination has to be removed and cleaned, you must use an
approved disinfectant to kill all harmful micro-organisms.
(5) The flight safety of the airplane, together with the safety of health and the prevention of bad
smells, must be your first consideration when you complete this task.
B. References
Reference Title
12-17-01-610-801 Waste Tank Servicing (P/B 301)
20-30-31 P/B 201 CLEANERS AND POLISHES - MAINTENANCE PRACTICES
38-32-01-400-801-001 Toilet Shroud Installation (P/B 401)
38-32-01-400-843-003 Toilet Shroud Installation (P/B 401)

Wiper (Cheesecloth, Gauze)

(Supersede BMS15-5
CL A)

E. Procedure
SUBTASK 05-51-12-110-002
WARNING
ALWAYS PUT ON RUBBER GLOVES BEFORE YOU DO MAINTENANCE ON
THE TOILET SYSTEM, OR TOUCH PARTS THAT TOUCHED WASTE
MATERIAL. FULLY CLEAN YOUR HANDS WITH SOAP AND WATER AFTER
MAINTENANCE IS COMPLETED. THE TOILET WASTE CAN CAUSE ILLNESS
AND INJURIES TO PERSONNEL.
(1) Put on protective clothing before you begin to clean up the blue water.
(2) Use a clean cotton cloth, G50316 or cotton wiper, G00034 to remove the blue water from the
contamination area.
NOTE: If a large quantity of liquid is to be removed, a suction pump should be used to drain
the contaminated area.
(3) Use approved cleaning agents and disinfectants when you clean areas where blue water
contamination has occurred, CLEANERS AND POLISHES - MAINTENANCE PRACTICES,
PAGEBLOCK 20-30-31/201.
(4) When blue water is found in the lavatory area, do the steps that follow:
(a) Remove laying blue water from all surfaces.
NOTE: Most of the blue water should drain out of the airplane through the floor drains
and the waste water system.
1) Use clean fresh water to dilute contaminated areas of the blue stain.
(b) If there are signs of blue water on the toilet tank, make sure you remove all blue water
stains from the toilet tank and all related components and connections.
NOTE: It is important that all blue stains are removed from the area. This will allow
accurate visual inspections to be done in the future.
(c) If blue water was found on the modular toilet, make sure all signs of blue water stains are
removed and the weep holes in the floor pan are free from blockage.
(d) Use a clean, moisture-free cotton cloth, G50316 or cotton wiper, G00034 to fully dry all
surfaces and components.
(e) Use a dry air supply to fully remove additional moisture from the contaminated areas
which are difficult to touch.
(f) If there are surface areas which remain with a blue stain, make a record of the precise
location.
NOTE: A record of a blue stain area can help to find the cause of a possible new leak of
blue water, should a leak occur in the future.
(5) If blue water is found in the electronic equipment compartment, do the steps that follow:
(a) Protect adjacent areas to the contaminated area, from the cleaning procedure, by the use
of polyethylene sheeting as a waterproof cover.
(b) Use clean fresh water to dilute contaminated areas of the blue stain.
(c) Use a clean cotton cloth, G50316 or cotton wiper, G00034 to remove laying blue water
from all areas shown during the toilet over-servicing inspection of the electronic
equipment compartment.
(d) If the airstair drip pan is contaminated by blue water, do the steps that follow:
1) Make sure the airstair drip pan is drained of liquid.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
2) Open this access panel:
Number Name/Location
117BL Forward Airstair Door
3) Fully clean the airstair drip pan and access panel with fresh water.
4) Make sure the drain in the access panel is free from blockage.
(e) Use a clean cloth to fully dry all surfaces and use a dry air supply to dry the areas which
are difficult to touch.
(f) If the area below the toilet tank shows signs of blue water contamination, fully clean the
drain tube, the ground flush hose or the drain valve control cable with fresh water.
NOTE: You must be most careful with the use of water in the electronic equipment
compartment; additional contamination must not occur.
(g) If the blue water contamination shows on the electronic racks and equipment, do the
steps that follow:
1) Remove blue water from all surfaces, cables and connectors.
2) Use a dry air supply to remove all moisture from the contaminated areas.
NOTE: Electrical cable looms can hold moisture between the separate wires. If
possible, open the wires in a contaminated cable when you dry the cable.
3) Remove all signs of blue water from tubes which could conduct moisture, such as
the pitot-static tubes, as necessary.
4) Do a check of contaminated connectors for blue water ingress and dry as
necessary.
NOTE: If you think a connector is contaminated with blue water, you must
disconnect and fully examine the connector and the related equipment
connector.
(h) Do an operational test of equipment which possibly could have been contaminated with
blue water.
(6) Do the servicing procedure for the system Waste Tank Servicing, TASK 12-17-01-610-801.

117A Electronic Equipment Access Door

05-51-12-200-801Toilet Over-Servicing Condition - InspectionPDF p. 915
2. Toilet Over-Servicing Condition - Inspection
A. General
(1) This inspection procedure is to be done when an over-service of the toilet system has occurred
or you think it has occurred.
NOTE: The term "over-service" is used to show that too much blue water has been used
during the servicing of the toilet system, and has spilled inside the airplane.
(2) It is possible for blue water contamination to occur in a single isolated area or more than one
area, dependent upon the amount of liquid spilled.
(3) A full visual inspection is necessary to confirm the extent of possible blue water contamination.
NOTE: Spilled liquid can use different flowpaths to disperse.
(4) It is recommended to do a check of the airplane records to see if there has been a spill of blue
water before and if blue stains remain.
NOTE: Unnecessary work can be avoided if knowledge of another over-servicing is available
for comparison.

05-51-13-211-801Galley Spill Conditional - InspectionPDF p. 919
2. Galley Spill Conditional - Inspection
A. General
(1) This inspection procedure is to be done when liquid has been spilled in the galley area.
NOTE: When a small amount of liquid is spilled, an inspection is not usually necessary.
(2) In the galley areas, a water (liquid) barrier is installed to contain liquid when it is spilled. To
protect the water barrier, vinyl mats cover the galley floor.
(3) In the adjacent entry and service door thresholds, waste water drains are installed to remove
liquids (gray water) from the floor. These drain holes must be kept free from blockages.
(4) The integrity of the water barrier seal, in the forward galley areas, is most important because
the location of the electronic equipment compartment is directly below the forward galley.
(5) A leak from the forward galley which has a damaged water barrier, into the compartment
below, could possibly cause serious damage to the electronic equipment. The result could be a
possible hazard to the flight safety of the airplane.
(6) In all areas where gray water contamination has to be removed and cleaned, you must use an
approved disinfectant to kill all harmful micro-organisms.
(7) The flight safety of the airplane, together with the safety of health and the prevention of bad
smells, must be your first consideration when you do this task.

05-51-14-210-801Mercury Spillage Conditional InspectionPDF p. 923
2. Mercury Spillage Conditional Inspection
A. References
Reference Title
25-80-00-000-801 Insulation Blanket Removal (P/B 401)
25-80-00-400-801 Insulation Blanket Installation (P/B 401)
B. General
SUBTASK 05-51-14-160-001
(1) A mercury spill must be considered hazardous, and immediate action must be taken to isolate,
inspect, and clean the aircraft.
(2) The corrosive action of mercury is very rapid in pitting and intergranular.
(3) Mercury amalgamates quickly with aluminum alloys at room temperature if the oxide film on
the aluminum has been scratched or damaged.
(a) Once a small area of aluminum has been amalgamated, corrosion and liquid metal
embrittlement occurs. This process is accelerated by moisture and particularly by salt
water.
(4) The amalgamation of stressed aluminum structure may also result in rapid cracking similar to
stress corrosion cracking.
(5) Mercury is not consumed in the amalgamation process. As the aluminum oxidizes, it separates
from the amalgam and the mercury continues to attack fresh aluminum.
(6) The presence of organic finishes, greases or a thick continuous oxide layer retards the
amalgamation process.
(7) When elemental mercury leaks on to an all-metallic structure, severe structural strength
degradation can occur.
(a) The rate of the diffusion of the mercury into a metal is related to the type of metal touched
by the mercury.
(b) The diffusion is also related to the type of finish protection on the metal.
(c) When the diffusion has started, it cannot be stopped.
(d) Structural degradation after a mercury spill is not always visually apparent until a load is
applied to the structure.
(8) The inspection, removal, or repair must be made before the next flight.
(9) Structural repairs are necessary if there are signs of mercury contamination.
(10) Make sure there is no detectable mercury in the airplane.
(a) Use mercury sniffers and X-ray equipment (if available) to detect mercury.
(b) The airplane is only clean when there is no detectable mercury.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
C. Personal Protection
SUBTASK 05-51-14-160-002
(1) Throughout the decontamination process follow these steps:
(a) Monitor the mercury vapor levels near the spill area and protect personnel from
exposure.
(b) Look for new free mercury deposits around the suspect spill area.
(c) Limit the number of persons around and on the airplane to the minimum required.
(d) Allow only persons trained in mercury spillage cleanup.
(2) Mercury vapor can cause effects in the central and peripheral nervous systems, lungs,
kidneys, skin and eyes in humans. Acute exposure to high concentrations of mercury vapor
causes severe respiratory damage, while chronic exposure to lower levels is primarily
associated with central nervous system damage. Chronic exposure to mercury is also
associated with behavioral changes and alterations in peripheral nervous system.
(a) Mercury Exposer Limits are based on local regulations. Refer to your local regulations for
applicable exposure limits.
1) The following exposure levels are also available for your reference:
NOTE: Check the web sites for the latest information and exposure limits.
a) Per the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA):
<1> For a 24 hours daily (continuous) exposer the safe limit for chronic
inhalation of elementary mercury is 0.3 µg/m³ (microgram per cubic
meter). This limit should be safe for 24 hour exposure of general
population.
<2> The Lowest-Observed Adverse Effect Level (LOAEL) is 25 µg/m³
(converted to LOAEL [ADJ] of 9 µg/m³). The LOAEL is based on an
8-hour TWA occupational exposure. LOAEL [ADJ] limit is based on an
8-hour per day and 40 hours per week TWA occupational exposure.
(Source http://www.epa.gov/iris/subst/0370.htm#refinhal).
b) Per the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA):
<1> Permissible exposure limit (PEL) for mercury vapor is 100 µg/m³ of air
as a ceiling limit. A worker's exposure to mercury vapor shall at no time
exceed this ceiling level.
<2> OSHA recognizes the National Institute for Occupational Safety and
Health (NIOSH) established recommended exposure limit (REL) for
mercury vapor of 50 µg/m³ as a TWA for up to a 10-hour workday and a
40-hour workweek.
<3> OSHA also recognizes American Conference of Governmental
Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) assigned mercury vapor threshold limit
value (TLV) of 25 µg/m³ as a TWA for a normal 8-hour workday and a
40-hour workweek. (Source
http://www.osha.gov/SLTC/healthguidelines/mercuryvapor/recognition.html)
(3) Large amounts of mercury will vaporize at normal temperatures.
(a) Ventilate enclosed space because the air mass can become dangerous to personal
health.
(4) Free mercury or amalgam must not be picked up by hand.
(5) Clean tools with soap and hot water or steam bath.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(a) Discard drill bits after use on structure contaminated by mercury.
(6) Mercury can attach easily to clothing.
(a) Use protective mats or cardboard to prevent contamination of clothing and the spread of
mercury to other areas.
(7) Mercury is highly toxic and spreads very easily from one surface to another by adhering to
hands, shoes, clothes, tools, etc.
(a) The following precautions for mercury spills should be strictly followed:
1) Avoid contact with surfaces suspected of being contaminated. Use wood or fiber
sheets to support body while working in the area.
2) Wear wing socks (shoe protectors) and protective (disposable) clothing in
contaminated area to prevent scratching metal surfaces. Properly dispose of socks
after use.
3) Do not wear clothing used in contaminated areas on jobs in uncontaminated areas.
Dispose of wing socks and protective clothing into unused metal container outside
of aircraft. Contact the Waste Management Service.
4) Wash shoes with soap and water. Clean all tools that have been used in
contaminated area with steam or hot water and soap. Discard any drill bits used on
mercury contaminated areas. Thoroughly clean vacuum cleaner, if used.
5) Always wash thoroughly with soap and water after contacting mercury. Keep hands
away from mouth. Do not eat, smoke, or blow nose without first washing your hands
thoroughly.
6) Appreciable amounts of mercury will vaporize at normal temperatures. A stagnant
air will become dangerous to personal health.
7) Do not use cleaning aids such as solvents, solids, or polishes on contaminated
areas. Such materials may promote corrosion.
8) If hands become contaminated with mercury while working with cleaning equipment,
do not touch any exposed metal in surrounding area, as you may contaminate it.
D. Isolation of the Mercury
SUBTASK 05-51-14-160-003
(1) Isolate the mercury spill area to prevent contamination to other areas.
(2) Evaluate the spill for cleanup.
NOTE: Depending on the amount and extent of the spill, consider using a specialized cleanup
company that has trained personnel for handling mercury spills and cleanup of
hazardous materials.
(3) Make a record of the general quantity of the mercury spilled.
(4) Make a record of the location where the mercury was spilled.
(5) When mercury is found on floor, do not remove coverings, access/inspection plates, screws,
rivets, bolts, etc., from floor until all free mercury is removed.
(6) Isolate the spilled mercury and avoid enlargement of the contaminated area. The following
precautions are advised:
(a) If mercury is found on the floor, do not remove coverings, access/inspection plates,
screws, rivets, bolts, etc., from the floor until all free mercury is removed.
1) Any hole which is left open in the contaminated area of the floor may allow mercury
to spread to structure underneath the floor.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(b) If hands become contaminated, do not touch any exposed metal in the surrounding area
in case it becomes contaminated.
(c) Mercury spreads easily from one surface to another by adhering to hands, shoes,
clothes, tools, etc. Keep traffic to a minimum in the contaminated area.
(d) Consider protecting uncontaminated areas by taping down protective material such as
plastic sheets or toweling. Plastic sheeting or toweling can also be taped over a
contaminated area to isolate it while equipment is being collected for the removal of
mercury.
E. Detection and Cleanup
SUBTASK 05-51-14-160-004
(1) Because of the urgency involved in removing mercury from the airplane, most of these
procedures utilize materials that are readily available locally. However, the use of some special
equipment is beneficial in ensuring that all traces of mercury are removed, and the sources of
supply for these items are as follows:
(a) Hg vacuum cleaner: Nilfisk of America Inc. (V57573).
(b) Sensing device (mercury sniffer): Beckman Industrial Corp. (V73138), or Sunshine
Scientific Instruments Inc. (V06030).
(c) Nickel-plated carbon-fiber brushes: International Research and Development Co.
(d) Fine copper wire brush: Produced locally or commercially available.
(e) Mercury sponge: J.T. Baker Chemical Co. (V70829). Volume
(2) A grayish-white powder or fuzzy coating on aluminum surfaces indicates the presence of
corrosion caused by spilled mercury.
(3) The presence of even small amounts of mercury can be detected by a sniffer.
NOTE: This is an electronic device that is sensitive to mercury vapor.
SUBTASK 05-51-14-160-005
(4) Inspect the metal floor, seat tracks, cargo rails, and adjacent structure for mercury and
corrosion.
(a) Inspect skin and internal structure below point of spillage.
(b) Also inspect lowest point in fuselage below cargo compartment floor if mercury spill has
occurred in cargo area.
NOTE: Mercury liquid will flow to lowest level.
(5) Inspect areas suspected of having mercury contamination using a 10X magnifying glass.
(a) If corrosion of aluminum has started there will be a light grayish “Christmas Tree” fuzz or
gray powdery dust deposit, and severe structural damage may follow.
(6) If corrosion is evident and cleanup cannot be completed immediately, coat contaminated area
with corrosion preventative compound or engine oil.
NOTE: This helps to slow down the corrosion rate and also helps to prevent spreading of
mercury contamination.
(7) When mercury spills occur in lower cargo compartment, use a portable X-ray machine (if
available) along the outside lower surface of the fuselage to check suspected hidden corrosion
areas between the skin, stringers, and frames below the floor.
(a) Droplets of mercury will show on a radiograph as small white spots.
(b) Corrosion and embrittlement will appear as tree-like forms completely penetrating a
structural component.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(c) While the basic X-ray exposure and film density parameters are acceptable to , it
is recommended to reverse the film and X-ray tube placement.
(d) X-Ray evaluation only needs to be performed in areas that are suspected to be
contaminated.
1) Special attention must be given to the area along joints and crevices, e.g.
skin/stringer joint, stringer clips.
WARNING
DO NOT GET MERCURY IN YOUR MOUTH, EYES, OR ON YOUR SKIN. DO
NOT BREATHE THE FUMES FROM THE MERCURY. WEAR PROTECTIVE
SPLASH GOGGLES AND GLOVES WHEN YOU CLEAN A MERCURY SPILL.
MERCURY IS POISONOUS AND CAN CAUSE INJURY TO PERSONS.
WARNING
FULLY REMOVE ALL MERCURY FROM THE AIRPLANE. MERCURY CAN
CAUSE INJURIES TO PERSONNEL, AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT.
(8) Remove all free mercury without delay. The following methods of removal are suggested, the
more primitive methods are less effective than those requiring special equipment, but any
possible method should be attempted whereby speed is essential.
(a) Use paper or cardboard troughs to scoop up the mercury.
(b) Use a high-powered mercury vacuum cleaner with a trap, if available. Figure 201
(Sheet 1) for a suggested method of making a trap.
1) Locate the vacuum outside the airplane in a well ventilated location to reduce the
possibility of contamination to other areas.
2) The size of the pickup hose from the container should be about ¼-inch in diameter
to increase the amount of suction applied to the mercury.
NOTE: Due to the weight of mercury, the container will catch the mercury before it
can enter the vacuum cleaner hose.
(c) An all rubber storage battery water syringe, or a medicine dropper, may be used to
remove mercury if the trap-type glass container and vacuum cleaner are not available.
(d) Cellulose tape may be used to pick up very tiny particles of mercury. General cleanup
and inspection (using equipment available) should be made immediately after spillage
occurs or is detected.
(e) A fine copper wire brush can also be used to pick up mercury. It is suggested that a
suitable brush could be manufactured locally by using the fine wires used in domestic
flexible electrical cable. The procedure for using the copper brush is as follows:
1) Use one of the special mercury pickup brushes that attract the mercury. Foam pads
are also commercially available that will pick up mercury.
2) Dip the brush in nitric acid (HN03) to clean the wires.
3) Dip the brush into water to remove the acid.
4) Dip the brush into alcohol to remove the water.
5) Pick up the mercury with the brush. Mercury adheres to the copper wires by forming
an amalgam. After the brush has collected a quantity of mercury it can be shaken
off into a suitable container, and the picking up process continued.
(9) Remove the insulation blankets in the spill area and discard them, do this task: Insulation
Blanket Removal, TASK 25-80-00-000-801.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(a) Also remove all of the insulation blankets that are downstream of the spill.
NOTE: Make sure you remove all blankets that go to the nearest lateral fluid dams.
(10) Where there is evidence of the presence of mercury in joints, between faying surfaces, or
trapped in any way between structural members, they must be disassembled as necessary to
permit complete removal of the mercury.
(11) Inspect bronze/brass control cable turnbuckle barrels for mercury discoloration. Replace if
slightest discoloration is detected.
SUBTASK 05-51-14-750-001
(12) Heat Cycling and Ventilation (optional):
(a)  is aware of the use of a heat cycle to vaporize mercury at the microscopic level.
1) This process has been used by the industry in an effort to completely eliminate
mercury from the airplane.
2) This process includes monitoring vapor levels at the elevated temperatures, and
venting the aircraft to remove the trace amounts
3) This process is for mercury removal process when visual indication is not entirely
possible.
(b) The heat and vent process is accomplished multiple times, reaching temperatures as
high as 138°F (59°C).
NOTE: External sources are exclusively used for heating. Aircraft air conditioning packs
and equipment cooling are not used to heat aircraft to ensure systems are
isolated and vapors are not cycled throughout clean areas. Upon reactivation of
aircraft, the aircraft air conditioning and the ECS are cycled to ensure vents are
cleared and cabin is clean.
1) Heating to such levels is more than 2.5 times the vaporization temperature (mercury
readily vaporizes at 55°F (13°C).
2) Six remote thermometers are used to monitor internal temperatures for 12-hour
periods to ensure aircraft structure reaches the elevated temperatures.
3) Following the heat, the aircraft is vented for 12 hours to clear the vapor overboard.
4) Each cycle of heat and ventilation can give significant drops in vapor levels at high
and low temperatures.
F. Put the Airplane Back to It's Usual Condition
SUBTASK 05-51-14-410-002
(1) Install the components that you removed or install replaceable parts.
(a) Do this task: Insulation Blanket Installation, TASK 25-80-00-400-801.

05-51-17-210-801Wheel Bearing FailurePDF p. 937
2. Wheel Bearing Failure
A. General
(1) This section gives an inspection procedure for landing gear wheels, brakes, axle sleeves, and
axles after a wheel bearing failure.
(2) The degradation of wheel bearing components can occur as follows:
(a) Lubrication that is incorrect or not sufficient
(b) A decrease of the wheel bearing preload
(c) Contamination in the bearing
(d) Other damage that occurs.
(3) When you operate with damaged wheel bearings, it will cause heat in the adjacent parts:
(a) The axles
(b) The axle sleeves
(c) The spacers
(d) The wheel hubs.
(4) These parts can have scores if the bearing damage causes a seizure and then causes rotation
that is relative to the adjacent parts.
(5) Do an inspection of the wheel bearings carefully during each tire change.
(6) The failure of a wheel bearing can be found by the symptoms or conditions that follow:
(a) Contamination of the wheel bearing grease with unwanted material.
(b) Metal particles or fragments in the area of the wheel and the brake
(c) The hubcap is damaged or is missing (main gear only)
(d) A wheel that is canted more than usual.
(e) The wheel and tire assembly are missing.

05-51-18-210-801Bird Strike and In-flight Hail Strike Conditional InspectionPDF p. 943
2. Bird Strike and In-flight Hail Strike Conditional Inspection
A. General
(1) All of the inspections are visual unless shown differently in the procedure.
(2) Examine the external surfaces of the airplane structure in the general area of the bird/in-flight
hail strike.
(a) If the initial inspection shows structural damage, then the internal structure must be
inspected.
(b) If the bird/in-flight hail struck the nose radome, the inside of the radome must be
inspected even if no damage is found on the exterior of the nose radome.
1) If the outer skin-to-core of the radome does not compress when you apply strong
finger pressure to impact area, then do the internal inspection at or before 3 flight
cycles.
(c) Also inspect the hydraulic, pneumatic, and other systems in the area of the bird/in-flight
hail strike for damage.
(3) When the conditional inspection tells you to "examine" a component, look for these conditions
(repair or replace components, if it is necessary):
(a) Cracks
(b) Pulled apart structure
(c) Loose paint (paint flakes)
(d) Twisted parts (distortion)
(e) Bent components
(f) Ruptures
(g) Loose fasteners
(h) Fasteners holes that became larger or longer
(i) Fasteners that have pulled out or are gone
(j) Delaminations
(k) Fiber breakouts
(l) Misalignment
(m) Interference
(n) Other signs of damage.
(4) If damage is found during these inspections, go to the related maintenance manual section for
the repair.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
B. References
Reference Title
12-40-04-100-801 Bird Strike Cleaning (P/B 201)

 ALL
(p) Examine the nose landing gear doors and linkage.
(q) Examine the main landing gear doors and linkage.

4) The pipes
5) The pulleys
6) The mechanical linkage
7) Refer to SRM 51-10-02 for the analysis and continued service of airplanes with hail
damage.
SUBTASK 05-51-18-210-004

SUBTASK 05-51-18-440-005

SUBTASK 05-51-18-440-006

(1) Install the components you removed or install replacement parts.
05-51-18-212-801Hail Strike on the Ground Conditional InspectionPDF p. 947
3. Hail Strike on the Ground Conditional Inspection
A. General
(1) This inspection is required if hail reported as GR 0.25 in. (6.35 mm) or greater in size strikes
the aircraft.
(a) If the GR hail struck the nose radome, the inside of the radome must be inspected even if
no damage is found on the exterior of the nose radome.
1) If the outer skin-to-core of the radome does not compress when you apply strong
finger pressure to impact area, then do the internal inspection at or before 3 flight
cycles.
(b) For GR hail less than 0.25 in. (6.35 mm), no inspection is required.
(2) This inspection is not required if GS hail strikes the aircraft.
(a) GS hail is defined as white, opaque grains of ice. The pellets are round or sometimes
conical and are less than 0.2 in. (5.1 mm) in diameter.

05-51-19-210-804Phase I InspectionPDF p. 953
2. Phase I Inspection
A. General
(1) Use of visual aids from the ground is acceptable to perform the following procedure.
(2) If a system malfunction is reported by the flight crew then a system check is required.
(3) Any requests for engineering analysis and repairs must contain the following information:
(a) Clearly defined damage:
1) Damage location defined with dimensioned on the production drawings and photos
for reference.
2) Damage extent.
3) Cause of damage.
(b) Proposed repair Plan.
(c) Any limitations - equipment, materials, etc.
(d) Status of the aircraft and airplane Return to Service date.
(e) Desired outcome (Permanent, Time Limited/Temporary, or Ferry Flight).
(4) Phase II Inspection may be deferred up to 50 flight cycles for the following conditions:
(a) No damage was found during Phase I Inspection.
(b) Damage was found and assessed/resolved accordingly during Phase I Inspection.

D. Phase I - Metallic Surfaces Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-019
(1) Perform a ground level inspection of Zones 1, 2, and 3 visible external metallic surfaces for
signs of lightning strike damage (Figure 202).
NOTE: Use of stands or ladders are not required.
(a) Look for visible signs of discolored paint, burn marks, melted areas, or holes in skin.
(b) If any damage is found, the damage must be assessed and/or repaired immediately per
the Structural Repair Manual (SRM) or approved method.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-020
(2) Perform a ground level inspection around the fuel areas of the wing torque box (Figure 201).
NOTE: A wing torque box includes the outboard wing, the wing center section, and the side of
the body structure. The outboard wing has upper and lower skin panels and front and
rear spar with ribs found perpendicular to the rear spar. The center section contains an
in-spar wing box and a wing-to-body interface structure.
(a) If any damage was found, assess and/or repair the damage per the SRM or approved
method.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-024
(3) Perform a ground level inspection of the wingtips or winglets metallic structure for lightning
strike damage.
(a) Examine the fuel vent outlet and surge tanks for signs of damage.
(b) If any damage was found, address the damage per the SRM or approved method.
E. Phase I - Composite Surfaces Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-037
(1) Perform a ground level inspection of Zones 1, 2, and 3 external composite surfaces for signs of
lightning strike damage (Figure 202).
NOTE: Use of stands or ladders are not required.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(a) Look for discolored paint, burns, punctures and delamination of composite honeycomb
sandwich structure.
(b) Examine the external composite surfaces from the ground of the nose radome for burns,
punctures, and pin holes in the composite honeycomb sandwich structure.
1) If damage is found, examine the internal surfaces and components under the nose
radome.
(c) If lightning strike damage is found, examine all composite structure in perimeter of
damaged area for signs of delamination.
1) Use instrumental or non-instrumental Non-Destructive Inspection (NDI) tap testing
to find composite structure delamination you cannot see.
a) For a tap test, use a solid metal disk and tap the area adjacent to the
damaged area lightly.
NOTE: If there is delamination, you will hear a sound that is different than the
sound of a solid bonded area. Refer to the Nondestructive Test
Manual.
2) If any damage was found, address the damage per the SRM or approved method.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-048
(2) Perform a ground level inspection of the wingtips or winglets composite structure.
(a) If any damage was found, address the damage per the SRM or approved method.
F. Phase I - System Components Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-051
(1) Perform a ground level inspection of the Angle of Attack (AOA) sensors, the pitot probes, static
ports, and the surrounding areas for damage.
(a) Look for damage to the AOA sensors.
1) If damage is found, do this task: Angle of Attack Sensor - Inspection,
TASK 34-21-05-200-801.
(b) Look for damage to the pitot probes.
1) If damage is found, do this task: Pitot Probe Detailed Inspection,
TASK 34-11-01-200-804.
(c) Look for damage to the static ports.
1) If damage is found, do this task: Static Port - Detailed Inspection,
TASK 34-11-02-200-803.
(d) If any damage is found around the AOA sensors, pitot probes and static ports.
1) The damage must be assessed and/or repaired per the SRM or approved method.
a) Look for burns, punctures, discolored paint, and general skin distortion.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-022
(2) Perform a ground level inspection of all external lights for lightning strike damage.
(a) Look for broken light assemblies, broken or cracked lenses, or other visible damage.
(b) Repair or replace damaged parts as necessary until the light functions properly.
(c) If damage was found on the Anti-Collision or Emergency Lights, do a test of the lights that
follow:
1) Do this task: Anti-Collision Lights - Operational Test, TASK 33-44-00-710-801.
2) Do this task: Emergency Lights - Operational Test, TASK 33-51-00-720-801.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
SUBTASK 05-51-19-700-008
(3) Perform a ground level inspection of the flight control components for signs of lightning strike
damage.
(a) If the flight control components show signs of lightning strike damage, perform a General
Visual Inspection (GVI) of these items:
1) Surface hinges.
2) Bearings.
3) Bondings.
(b) If no damage is found, do a basic operational check of the flight controls as follows:
NOTE: If the flight controls operate correctly after you do these steps, no more
inspections are necessary.
1) Move the rudder, control wheel and control column in both directions.
2) Make sure that there is full travel and the flight controls move freely.
NOTE: Hold the nose wheel during the rudder check to prevent nose wheel
movement. You can hold the nose wheel if you put in the steering lockout
pin or remove the torsion link pin.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-720-005
(4) If the rudder system did not operate correctly during the operational check of the flight controls
steps above, do a functional test of the rudder system.
(a) Do this task: Rudder Trim System Test, TASK 27-21-00-700-819-002.
(b) Do this task: Rudder Pedal Forces Test, TASK 27-21-00-700-816-002.
(c) Do this task: Rudder Travel Test, TASK 27-21-00-700-817-002.
(d) Do this task: Rudder Centering Test, TASK 27-21-00-700-815-002.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-720-006
(5) If the elevator system did not operate correctly during the operational check of the flight
controls steps above, do a functional test of the elevator system.
(a) Do this task: Elevator Control Column Override - Operational Test,
TASK 27-31-00-710-802.
(b) Do this task: Elevator Tab Control System - Operational Test, TASK 27-31-00-700-815.
(c) Do this task: Elevator and Elevator Trim Control System - Operational Test,
TASK 27-31-00-710-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-720-007
(6) If the aileron system did not operate correctly during the operational check of the flight controls
steps above, do a functional test of the ailerons.
(a) Do this task: Aileron - Response (Operational) Test, TASK 27-11-00-710-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-210-025
(7) Perform a ground level inspection of the Static Dischargers for lightning strike damage.
(a) If any Static Dischargers are damaged or missing, assess with: Static Discharger
Inspection, TASK 23-61-00-210-801.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
G. External Wire Shields Detailed Inspection
SUBTASK 05-51-19-211-016
(1) Examine the following:
NOTE: If the lightning strike attach points can not be identified, then the external wire shield
examination is not required.
NOTE: If there are no wire shield termination(s) in the area of the attach points, then the
external wire shield examination is not required.
(a) In the area of the lightning strike attach points, examine the wire shield terminations.
(b) If the flight crew has reported a problem with any system after the lightning strike,
examine the wire shield terminations for that systems wiring.
(c) If damage is found at wire shield termination(s), check the full length of the wire bundle.
(d) Repair any damage found and do an operational check of the system that had the
damage.
H. System Internal Test
SUBTASK 05-51-19-700-006
(1) If a lightning strike caused a system malfunction, do a full test of the defective system.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-700-007
(2) If a magnetic compass malfunction is reported in the maintenance log, do a check of the
standby magnetic compass:
(a) Do this task: Standby Magnetic Compass System (Spot Check) - Inspection,
TASK 34-23-00-730-801.
1) If the result is not in limits, do this task: Standby Magnetic Compass - Degaussing,
TASK 34-23-00-820-803.
NOTE: It is not necessary to do one of these methods this time: Standby Magnetic
Compass - Compass Rose or Inertial Reference System (IRS) Method,
TASK 34-23-00-820-802 or Standby Magnetic Compass Swing - Standby
Compass Calibrator (SCC) Method, TASK 34-23-00-820-801.
(b) Do this task again to make sure the result is in the limits: Standby Magnetic Compass
System (Spot Check) - Inspection, TASK 34-23-00-730-801.
1) If the result is not in limits, do one of these tasks: Standby Magnetic Compass -
Compass Rose or Inertial Reference System (IRS) Method,
TASK 34-23-00-820-802 or Standby Magnetic Compass Swing - Standby Compass
Calibrator (SCC) Method, TASK 34-23-00-820-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-710-033
(3) Make sure that the fuel quantity system is accurate.
(a) Do the operational test for the Fuel Quantity Indication System (FQIS) type on your
airplane, do this task: Operational Test - Fuel Quantity Indicating System,
TASK 28-41-00-710-801.
(b) If the FQIS test shows any problems, do this task: Comparison Check - Fuel Quantity
Indicating System (FQIS) with the Fuel Measuring Sticks, TASK 28-41-00-720-801.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-710-036
(4) If the rudder or vertical stabilizer had a lightning strike, do these steps:
(a) Look for leaks from the rudder hydraulic aluminum return tubing aft of the aft pressure
bulkhead.
EFFECTIVITY
 ALL
(b) If leaks are found, replace components that have leaks.
SUBTASK 05-51-19-710-037
(5) If the elevator or horizontal stabilizer had a lightning strike, do these steps:
(a) Look for leaks from the elevator hydraulic aluminum return tubing aft of the aft pressure
bulkhead.
(b) If leaks are found, replace components that have leaks.
